facts.statement: The genus Pteranodon was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1876.
facts.quote: authority: Marsh, 1876

facts.statement: Pteranodon fossils date to the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Santonian to Campanian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous (Santonian-Campanian),

facts.statement: Pteranodon lived during the Late Cretaceous in North America, specifically in present-day Kansas, Nebraska, Wyoming, South Dakota, and Alabama.
facts.quote: They lived during the late Cretaceous geological period of North America in present-day Kansas, Nebraska, Wyoming, South Dakota and Alabama.

facts.statement: More than 1,200 specimens of Pteranodon are known to science, many of which are well-preserved with nearly complete skulls and articulated skeletons.
facts.quote: More fossil specimens of Pteranodon have been found than any other pterosaur, with about 1,200 specimens known to science, many of them well preserved with nearly complete skulls and articulated skeletons.

facts.statement: Pteranodon was the first pterosaur species discovered outside of Europe.
facts.quote: Pteranodon was the first pterosaur found outside of Europe.

facts.statement: The first fossils of Pteranodon were found by Othniel Charles Marsh in either 1870 or 1871 in the Smoky Hill Chalk deposits of western Kansas.
facts.quote: Its fossils first were found by Othniel Charles Marsh in either 1870 or 1871, in the Late Cretaceous Smoky Hill Chalk deposits of western Kansas.

facts.statement: The first specimens collected by Marsh consisted of partial wing bones and a tooth from the fish Xiphactinus, which Marsh mistakenly thought belonged to the pterosaur.
facts.quote: These first specimens, YPM 1160 and YPM 1161, consisted of partial wing bones, as well as a tooth from the prehistoric fish Xiphactinus, which Marsh mistakenly believed to belong to this new pterosaur

facts.statement: The first Pteranodon skull was found on May 2, 1876, along the Smoky Hill River in Kansas by Samuel Wendell Williston, a collector working for Marsh.
facts.quote: the first Pteranodon skull was found on May 2, 1876, along the Smoky Hill River in Wallace County (now Logan County), Kansas, USA, by Samuel Wendell Williston, a fossil collector working for Marsh.

facts.statement: Two distinct morphs of Pteranodon specimens have been found, which are thought to represent males and females.
facts.quote: Two distinct morphs of Pteranodon specimen have been found, that are thought to represent males and females.

facts.statement: Male Pteranodon attained wingspans of 5.6 to 7.6 meters, while females were smaller, averaging 3.8 meters.
facts.quote: Males attained wingspans of 5.6 - 7.6 m; females were smaller, averaging 3.8 m.

facts.statement: The crests of male Pteranodon were far larger than those of females.
facts.quote: The crests of males were far larger than those of females.

facts.statement: Pteranodon belongs to the family Pteranodontidae and the clade Pteranodontia, which also includes nyctosaurids.
facts.quote: Pteranodon is part of the family Pteranodontidae, part of the clade Pteranodontia, which also includes nyctosaurids.

facts.statement: Pteranodontians form the clade Pteranodontoidea alongside ornithocheiromorphs, which falls under the suborder Pterodactyloidea.
facts.quote: Pteranodontians form a larger clade, Pteranodontoidea, alongside ornithocheiromorphs, and that clade falls under the suborder Pterodactyloidea.

facts.statement: It is debated whether P. sternbergi and P. maiseyi should be classified as a separate genus, Geosternbergia.
facts.quote: Some researchers have suggested the latter two as a genus of their own, Geosternbergia, though this is the subject of some debate.

facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Williston was the first scientist to critically evaluate all Pteranodon species previously classified by Cope and Marsh.
facts.quote: Williston was also the first scientist to critically evaluate all of the Pteranodon species classified by Cope and Marsh.

facts.statement: In 1903, Williston revised the number of valid Pteranodon species from seven down to three.
facts.quote: In 1903, Williston revisited the question of Pteranodon classification, and revised his earlier conclusion that there were seven species down to just three.

facts.statement: Williston considered the species P. comptus and P. nanus to be specimens of the genus Nyctosaurus.
facts.quote: He considered both P. comptus and P. nanus to be specimens of Nyctosaurus

facts.statement: In 1910, Eaton published the first detailed description of the entire Pteranodon skeleton known at that time.
facts.quote: In 1910, Eaton became the first scientist to publish a more detailed description of the entire Pteranodon skeleton, as it was known at the time.

facts.statement: Eaton recognized only three valid species of Pteranodon: P. occidentalis, P. ingens, and P. longiceps.
facts.quote: In the end, Eaton recognized only three valid species: P. occidentalis, P. ingens, and P. longiceps.

facts.statement: Harksen classified specimens with upright crests as the new species Pteranodon sternbergi in 1966.
facts.quote: The discovery of specimens with upright crests, classified by Harksen in 1966 as the new species Pteranodon sternbergi, complicated the situation even further.

facts.statement: Miller concluded that all Pteranodon species except those based on skulls (P. longiceps and P. sternbergi) were nomina dubia.
facts.quote: Miller concluded that all Pteranodon species except the two based on skulls (P. longiceps and P. sternbergi) must be considered nomena dubia and abandoned.

facts.statement: Miller named the subgenus Occidentalia for the species P. eatoni, which was formerly associated with P. occidentalis.
facts.quote: Miller named the subgenus Occidentalia for P. eatoni, the skull formerly associated with P. occidentalis.

facts.statement: Miller expanded the concept of Pteranodon to include Nyctosaurus as a fourth subgenus.
facts.quote: Miller further expanded the concept of Pteranodon to include Nyctosaurus as a fourth subgenus.

facts.statement: In 1984, Schoch published a revision that returned to Marsh's classification, making P. longiceps a synonym of P. ingens.
facts.quote: In 1984, Robert Milton Schoch published another revision that essentially returned to Marsh's original classification scheme, most notably sinking P. longiceps as a synonym of P. ingens.

facts.statement: The average adult male Pteranodon had a wingspan of 5.6 meters.
facts.quote: The wingspan of an average adult male Pteranodon was 5.6 m.

facts.statement: Adult female Pteranodon averaged a wingspan of 3.8 meters.
facts.quote: Adult females were much smaller, averaging 3.8 m in wingspan.

facts.statement: A large male specimen (USNM 50130) of P. longiceps is estimated to have a wingspan of 6.25 to 6.5 meters, a body length of 2.6 meters, and a mass of 50 kg.
facts.quote: A large specimen of Pteranodon longiceps, USNM 50130, is estimated to have a wingspan of 6.25 - 6.5 m, body length of 2.6 m and body mass of 50 kg.

facts.statement: The largest known Pteranodon specimens had wingspans between 7.25 and 7.6 meters.
facts.quote: Even larger specimens had wingspans of 7.25 - 7.6 m.

facts.statement: Females had short, rounded crests and wide pelvic canals, while males had narrow hips and large crests likely used for display.
facts.quote: Size aside, females were distinguished by their short, rounded head crests and wide pelvic canals, whereas males had narrow hips and very large head crests, likely serving a display function.

facts.statement: Methods for estimating the mass of large male Pteranodon (wingspan ~7m) have been notoriously unreliable, producing widely varying estimates.
facts.quote: Methods used to estimate the mass of large male Pteranodon specimens (those with wingspans of about 7 meters) have been notoriously unreliable, producing a wide range of estimates.

facts.statement: In 2010, Witton and Habib argued that the 93 kg mass estimate is too high and that 20–35 kg is a more realistic upper limit.
facts.quote: In a review of pterosaur size estimates published in 2010, Mark Witton and Michael Habib argued that the largest estimate of 93 kg is much too high and an upper limit of 20–35 kg is more realistic.

facts.statement: Unlike earlier pterosaurs, Pteranodon possessed toothless beaks similar to those of birds.
facts.quote: Unlike earlier pterosaurs, such as Rhamphorhynchus and Pterodactylus, Pteranodon had toothless beaks, similar to those of birds.

facts.statement: The Pteranodon upper jaw was longer than the lower jaw and curved upward.
facts.quote: The upper jaw, which was longer than the lower jaw, was curved upward

facts.statement: Alexander Kellner assigned a specimen with a unique beak form to the distinct genus Dawndraco in 2010.
facts.quote: The unique form of the beak in this specimen led Alexander Kellner to assign it to a distinct genus, Dawndraco, in 2010.

facts.statement: Pteranodon crests consisted of frontal skull bones projecting upward and backward.
facts.quote: These crests consisted of skull bones (frontals) projecting upward and backward from the skull.

facts.statement: Males of the older species P. sternbergi had vertical crests with broad forward projections, while descendants like P. longiceps evolved narrower, backward-projecting crests.
facts.quote: Male Pteranodon sternbergi, the older species of the two described to date, had a more vertical crest with a broad forward projection, while their descendants, Pteranodon longiceps, evolved a narrower, more backward-projecting crest.

facts.statement: Females of both Pteranodon species were smaller and had small, rounded crests.
facts.quote: Females of both species were smaller and bore small, rounded crests.

facts.statement: The neural spines of Pteranodon vertebrae were narrow.
facts.quote: The neural spines of Pteranodon's vertebrae were narrow.

facts.statement: Pteranodon pelvic bones were fused to the synsacrum, which included at least two dorsal, sacral, and the first caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: The pelvic bones were fused to the synsacrum, a mass of vertebrae that included at least two dorsal vertebrae, the sacral vertebrae, and the first caudal vertebra.

facts.statement: Pteranodon scapulae were oriented to brace each other via fusion with coracoids, increasing flight integrity.
facts.quote: Pteranodon's scapulae were oriented in such a way that each one braces the other, due to their fusion with the coracoids, providing increased integrity during flight.

facts.statement: Pteranodon hind feet had four metatarsals tipped with less curved claws.
facts.quote: Pteranodon's hind feet had four metatarsals, which were tipped with less curved claws.

facts.statement: Pteranodon likely flew in a manner similar to modern albatrosses.
facts.quote: The wing shape of Pteranodon suggests that it would have flown rather like a modern-day albatross.

facts.statement: Pteranodon had a high aspect ratio of 9:1, which is similar to the 8:1 ratio found in albatrosses.
facts.quote: This is based on the fact that Pteranodon had a high aspect ratio (wingspan to chord length) similar to that of the albatross — 9:1 for Pteranodon, compared to 8:1 for an albatross.

facts.statement: Recent research suggests Pteranodon relied on thermal soaring, a behavior distinct from modern seabirds but similar to continental flyers and the extinct Pelagornis.
facts.quote: However, a more recent study suggests that it relied on thermal soaring, unlike modern seabirds but much like modern continental flyers and the extinct Pelagornis.

facts.statement: The mode of terrestrial locomotion for Pteranodon has been debated, specifically regarding whether it was bipedal or quadrupedal.
facts.quote: Historically, terrestrial locomotion in Pteranodon, as in pterosaurs overall, has been the subject of debate, chiefly the matter of whether or not they were bipedal or quadrupedal.

facts.statement: In 2004, Chatterjee and Templin proposed that pterosaurs like Pteranodon walked quadrupedally but used a bipedal takeoff, though this is considered unlikely.
facts.quote: In 2004, Sankar Chatterjee and R. J. Templin proposed a dual system, wherein pterosaurs walked quadrupedally most of the time, but opted for a bipedal takeoff.

facts.statement: Fossil trackways suggest that Pteranodon was a quadruped.
facts.quote: Trackways suggest that pterosaurs like Pteranodon were quadrupedal.

facts.statement: Pteranodon ate fish, evidenced by fossilized fish bones in one specimen's stomach and a fish bolus in the jaws of specimen AMNH 5098.
facts.quote: The diet of Pteranodon is known to have included fish; fossilized fish bones have been found in the stomach area of one Pteranodon, and a fossilized fish bolus has been found between the jaws of another Pteranodon, specimen AMNH 5098.

facts.statement: Fish likely made up the majority of the Pteranodon diet, though it may have also consumed invertebrates.
facts.quote: Numerous other specimens also preserve fragments of fish scales and vertebrae near the torso, indicating that fish made up a majority of the diet of Pteranodon (though they may also have taken invertebrates).

facts.statement: In 1994, Bennett suggested that Pteranodon could dive by folding its wings back, similar to modern gannets, due to its heavy head, neck, and shoulder structure.
facts.quote: In 1994, Bennett noted that the head, neck, and shoulders of Pteranodon were as heavily built as diving birds, and suggested that they could dive by folding back their wings like the modern gannet.

facts.statement: The function of the Pteranodon skull crest has been a subject of scientific debate.
facts.quote: Pteranodon was notable for its skull crest, though the function of this crest has been a subject of debate.

facts.statement: Display is considered the primary function of the Pteranodon crest, with other functions being secondary.
facts.quote: Therefore, display was probably the main function of the crest, and any other functions were secondary.

facts.statement: In 1910, George Francis Eaton proposed that the crest served as an aerodynamic counterbalance or a muscle attachment point.
facts.quote: Scientific interpretations of the crest's function began in 1910, when George Francis Eaton proposed two possibilities: an aerodynamic counterbalance and a muscle attachment point.

facts.statement: In 1943, Dominik von Kripp suggested the crest functioned as a rudder, a hypothesis supported by later researchers.
facts.quote: In 1943, Dominik von Kripp suggested that the crest may have served as a rudder, an idea embraced by several later researchers.

facts.statement: After ruling out other theories, sexual display is the best-supported hypothesis for the function of the Pteranodon crest.
facts.quote: With these hypotheses ruled out, the best-supported hypothesis for crest function seems to be as a sexual display.

facts.quote: Se han encontrado más especímenes fósiles de Pteranodon que de cualquier otro pterosaurio, con cerca de 1,200 especímenes conocidos por la ciencia actual

facts.statement: In 2017, Bennett described FHSM 17956, the smallest known Pteranodon specimen, an incomplete right wing from the Smoky Hill Chalk.

facts.statement: The average wingspan of an adult male Pteranodon was 5.6 meters.

facts.statement: Weight estimates for large male Pteranodon (wingspans near 7 meters) range from 20 kg to 93 kg.

facts.statement: A possible third species, named Geosternbergia maysei in 2010, is known from the Sharon Springs Member of the Pierre Shale Formation in Kansas, Wyoming, and South Dakota, dating to 81.5 to 80.5 million years ago.
